slides.topic: Coronary Artery Disease & Anti-anginal Drugs — page 2
slides.text:
Learning Outcomes
By the end of the lecture, you should be able to:
• Define coronary artery disease (CAD)
• Describe the pathophysiology of atherosclerosis
• Explain how and imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply 
and demand contributes to angina. 
• Describe the clinical features of stable angina
• Explain the pharmacological principles/targets underlying the 
treatment of stable angina. 
• Describe the mechanisms of action of major anti-anginal drugs
• β-adrenoceptor blockers 
• Organic nitrates 
• Calcium-channel blockers
• Ivabradine 
• Others -nicorandil and ranolazine, trimetazididne

slides.topic: Coronary Artery Disease & Anti-anginal Drugs — page 7
slides.text:
Key to diagram
1. Endothelial damage (hypertension, smoking, diabetes)→ ↑ permeability to LDL, ↓NO 
production 
2. Monocytes adhere to adhesion molecules (eg vascular cell adhesion molecule -1/ VCAM1) 
and infiltrates into intima
3. Monocytes differentiate into macrophages which contain scavenger receptors on surface
4. LDL (low density lipoprotein) becomes oxidised (Ox-LDL) by free radicals released by 
macrophages
5. Scavenger receptors recognise oxidised LDL. Ox-LDL engulfed by macrophages. 
6. These become foam cells containing cholesterol  derived form LDL –
Foam cells + inflammatory cells create Fatty streak 
7. Macrophages release cytokines such as interleukins (eg IL-1β, TNFα)
8. Vascular smooth muscle cells migrate into the intima from the medial layer (Media) & 
proliferate. 
9. Connective tissue eg collagen, elastin is deposited. 
10. Connective tissue and vascular smooth muscle cell form a fibrous cap around the core of 
the plaque 
11. Core of the plaque: foam cells, cellular debris and fatty material released from dead foam 
cells.
12. Rupture of fibrous cap leads to platelet adhesion and aggregation and  thrombus (blood 
clot) formation leading to narrowing of lumen and ischaemic disease

slides.topic: Coronary Artery Disease & Anti-anginal Drugs — page 10
slides.text:
In Stable angina, why is there pain only in physical 
exertion or excitement etc ?
• At rest, blood flow to the myocardium is sufficient through 
the narrowed coronary artery. Enough O2 is supplied
• During exercise etc - inability of coronary blood flow to 
increase sufficiently, to meet the increased metabolic 
demands of the heart (increased O2 requirement during 
exercise, excitement).

A. Coronary blood flow cannot increase sufficiently to meet oxygen demand 
B. During exercise, myocardial oxygen demand increases 
C. Atherosclerotic plaque develops in a coronary artery 
D. Coronary artery lumen becomes narrowed 
E. Chest discomfort/pain (angina) occurs 
F. Myocardial ischaemia develops 
Arrange these events in the correct order on how a patient develops chest pain during 
exercise
Which two physiological factors could you pharmacologically target to reduce angina?
•
Reduced myocardial blood supply
•
Increased O2 demand/consumption
Answer:
1. Atherosclerotic plaque develops in a coronary artery
2. Coronary artery lumen becomes narrowed
3. During exercise, myocardial oxygen demand increases
4. Coronary blood flow cannot increase sufficiently to meet oxygen demand
5. Myocardial ischaemia develops
6. Chest discomfort/pain (angina) occurs

Normal heart derives 2/3rd of ATP from fatty acid oxidation (FAO). 1/3 from glucose 
oxidation.
FAO requires a greater amount of O2 than glucose metabolism to produce an equivalent 
amount of ATP (Glucose metabolism is ‘oxygen sparing’ ).
In myocardial ischaemia when there is a low availability of O2,  glucose oxidation is more 
favourable than FAO .
Trimetazidine shifts the myocardial energy source from FAO to glucose oxidation,  
reducing O2 demand
Trimetazidine (TMZ):  Fatty Acid oxidation inhibitor
main ATP sources in 
normal conditions
Trimetazidine is also has cytoprotective effects on the heart cell, . reducing acidosis, and preventing 
the accumulation of harmful byproducts of fatty acid metabolism during ischemic conditions.

Long-term management aims:
Improving quality of life 
Preventing angina episodes
Reducing the risk of MI
Life style adjustments: Diet and exercise, stopping smoking etc
Preventive Medications (reduce risk of MI or heart failure):
• Antiplatelet Agents (Aspirin, Clopidogrel): Help prevent formation of blood clots, reduce risk of MI
• Statins (e.g. Atorvastatin): Lower cholesterol levels, reduce inflammation, and stabilize 
atherosclerotic plaques.
• ACE Inhibitors/ARBs (e.g., Lisinopril, Losartan): Lower blood pressure, reduce workload on heart, 
and protects kidneys, especially in patients with diabetes or hypertension.
Interventional Procedures
• Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI):  (angioplasty 
and stenting)
• Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG)
